content: “Hey, honey, you’re not going to be able to sleep tonight if you don’t start shutting things down soon!” After 36 years of marriage, my husband knows me well. He’s absolutely right, but I still sometimes want to keep pushing until bedtime. The way of wisdom is to stop consciously, set the work aside, and engage in the repetitive, mundane wind-down of the day. The work will still be there tomorrow, and I can trust God for new mercies to finish when morning comes (Lamentations 3:22–23). Our habits of rest reveal what we trust. While our need for sleep, recreation, and downtime weighs on our very physical, very finite bodies, we often resist submitting to our limitations. Substituting entertainment for true rest, we become passive consumers of endlessly streaming content that devours our time. Paradoxically, we crave rest and engage in ceaseless striving after things we hope will satisfy the desires of our heart. This is an ongoing battle for me, and I know I’m not alone. Our society values activity and busyness. We spend our hours and days going and doing, always with one eye on the clock. We reward tireless resilience with job promotions and earnest admiration. In our fervor for achievement, we may forget that rest is necessary for quality work to continue — and that rest can teach our hearts to trust God. Rest Reveals the Heart Psalm 127:1–2 is a reminder for our caffeinated and sleep-deprived souls that progress depends not solely on the work of our own hands but on God’s gracious provision: Unless the L ORD builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the L ORD watches over the city, the watchman stays awake in vain. It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep. Note that the psalmist illustrates a right and a wrong way to work. He makes three important points for the restless. 1. The Lord builds the house. God builds the ministry, the family, and the career. We work in cooperation with the Lord, and he watches over us and our work. The point is not that we shouldn’t work heartily at whatever we do (Colossians 3:23). Rather, our security is found in God, not in our efforts. Knowing our frame, remembering that we are dust, God commands us to observe regular patterns of rest, not only for our physical health but also as an acknowledgment of our dependence upon him (Psalm 103:14). 2. The Lord watches over the city. Whether we’re closing our eyes or closing our laptop and office door at the end of the day, when we leave the results of our work in God’s hands, we demonstrate trust in him. “He who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep,” the psalmist writes (Psalm 121:4). God is your keeper, too. Entrusting our work to the Lord prevents it from becoming an idol. In our glad contemplation of work well done, we remember that he is both giver and gift. Our work is evidence of his power and goodness. 3. The Lord gives sleep to his beloved. Anyone who has spent a night sleepless from worry knows our bodies are not designed to run on anxious adrenaline. Insomnia has many causes and may not indicate a spiritual problem, but God often uses physical symptoms to reveal our spiritual condition. A steady diet of “the bread of anxious toil” (Psalm 127:2) starves us of what we need most: the ability to rest in God. When we rest, we accept our God-given limits. We hand the controls over to him. We lay aside our disordered loves, and we choose to believe the Father’s delight in Christ is also for us, his treasured children: “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). Because it can feel entirely unnatural, we may need to approach rest as a learned behavior, a habit of holiness, a spiritual discipline that we “put on” in the same way Paul exhorted the Colossians to clothe themselves with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience (Colossians 3:12). Such discipline is worth the effort; when we rest, we proclaim
author: Michele Morin

title: What We Get Wrong About the Tears of Jesus
summary: Was Jesus’s grief at Lazarus’s tomb over his friend’s death or the response of the mourners? Pastor John explains how Jesus’s perfect emotions captured his indignation over unbelief. Listen Now
content: Audio Transcript “Jesus wept” (John 11:35). It’s the shortest verse in the Bible. We read it together in the Navigators Bible Reading Plan yesterday. But it’s so brief we can pass it too quickly. Maybe we pass over it because we think we know what it means. Jesus’s friend Lazarus died. Jesus wept because his friend was gone. But what if we got that wrong? Or, what if we mistakenly thought his emotions were simple when they were complex? What if Jesus wept not simply in the loss of death but from a frustration with the living? Today on Ask Pastor John: what we get wrong about the tears of Jesus. Henry, a listener, writes in with a timely question on John 11:35. “Pastor John, thank you for taking my question today. I’d like to ask you about John 11:35. Why do you think Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus? One way to read this account is that he’s simply sharing in Mary and Martha’s sorrows over his death. But I wonder if something deeper is going on here. Jesus already planned to raise Lazarus, and he even told his disciples he was going to do it in John 11:11–15. “So, my questions are these two: First, why does Jesus ask, ‘Where have you laid him?’ Was he simply asking to be taken to the tomb? When they answer, ‘Lord, come and see,’ it’s almost like they still don’t appreciate who he is as the Messiah. And that is my second question: This whole event leaves me wondering if this weeping is more like Jesus’s weeping over Jerusalem in Luke 19:41 — weeping because he is heartbroken over the city’s unbelief. Is it a stretch to connect these two moments? Is Jesus grieving the dead Lazarus? Or is he grieving the unbelief of the living?” Jesus’s Mingled Emotions I doubt that any of Jesus’s emotions were simple. I think they were always complex. We finite creatures have emotions that respond to one or two, maybe three, happy or painful aspects of a situation. So, we may feel sorrow and joy mingled because, say, a very old saint has just gone to be with the Lord, and we will miss him, and yet we’re so happy for him. But Jesus could see every angle, every imaginable aspect of a situation, some of which called for very different emotions. So, I doubt that he ever had a simple emotion. For example, in Mark 3:1–5, there’s this man with a withered hand in the synagogue, and the people are watching to see if Jesus would heal him so that they could accuse Jesus. Can you imagine? They don’t give a hoot about this man’s pain. All they want is to accuse Jesus if he heals him. And in verse 5, it says, “He looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart.” And that’s what I mean by complex emotions: anger and grief perfectly mingled in the sinless heart of Jesus. Another example would be that he looked on unbelieving Jerusalem and wept: “Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes” (Luke 19:42). But in Luke 10:21, it says Jesus “rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said, ‘I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will.’” He could weep and rejoice over the wise and bitter providence of God. So, we come to John 11 and the death of Lazarus. And I think Henry, who’s sending us this question, is right when he says Jesus’s tears in John 11 aren’t just about sharing our human grief — that maybe he is genuinely mourning their spiritual blindness. Yes, and I’m going to say not just mourning — he’s indignant. Divine Love and Wisdom The story begins in John 11:1–6 with Mary and Martha sending words to Jesus that their brother Lazarus is very sick. Jesus waits two more days before going and intentionally lets Lazarus die. He says in John 11:14–15, “Lazarus has died, and for your sake I am glad that I was not there, so that you may believe.” That’s an amazing statement: “I let him die for the sake of your faith.” “They needed to

title: Can’t You Just Help Me?

content: Several times now, I have been out in creation with unbelievers, speaking to them of eternal matters, and, passing by a dying branch at the base of a tree, I have picked it up and said, “This is your life apart from Christ.” Speaking about their souls, Jesus’s illustration is irresistible. The conversation goes something like this: Jesus gives us this illustration. He looks you in the eye and says that he is the tree (to augment the illustration slightly), and you are the branch. Look up and see the branches above us, beautiful leaves waving, healthy in their vibrant greens, bearing evidence of life. And then there is this branch. Dry. Leafless. Withered. Why? Because it is detached from the source of its life. Cut off from the one it was made to have communion with. And so, it lies here, detached from its purpose and severed from the only thing that can make it flourish. Jesus claims to be man’s source. He claims to be the Tree to whom you belong. In relationship with him, you have life. Apart from him, he teaches, you spend life withering. I usually pause to let the claim have its proper space. I ask what they think of such an assertion. I give them an opportunity to respond. I have often expected indifference or offense, but I have consistently been met with quiet consideration or outright acknowledgment that such an illustration made sense to them. Or at least they would like to hear more. So I go on to wonder aloud with them. What is it like to be a branch fallen from the tree that is, as Jesus says, withering ? Don’t you know? Need we ask? The restlessness, the fatal dryness, the looming death. The reaching out to anything and everything for life — except for the tree standing beside and over us. Him we do not want. Him we can do without. We can make it our own way. The adverb is different, but the end is the same — restless withering, drunken withering, religious, secular, or thoughtless withering . Some overdose on pleasure. Others get high on their own morality. Still others distract themselves from death’s shadow creeping over them with fantasy football and rounds of golf. But for all that, withering. But Jesus himself asserts that he is the Tree. He is the one we were made for; in him alone can we find the life that haunts us in still and sober moments. Be grafted to him through repentance and faith, be attached to him by the Spirit of the living God, have his words live in you, direct you, amaze you, and dead things will come to life. And what will it be on that day, I am compelled to continue, for those dry and fruitless branches who refused life in him? They will be gathered and thrown into the fire and burned as useless things. But Jesus came that you might have otherwise. He told us his mission was to bring life — life abundantly . Imagine the branch grafted to the tree, suddenly infused with life and purpose and the vital sap of God’s own Spirit. We are as branches; the Father, Son, and Spirit are the source of everlasting life. With him, we flourish though all may seem to go poorly. Without him, only sapped wood remains. Would you like to know more about this Jesus? Now, I tell you this to highlight one of many places where the Bible addresses the interiority of man and its solution: God. I want you to see how dangerous the alternative answers found in modern therapeutic culture are to our souls and our churches. It is a scourge, especially to this inward age, not because a therapeutic culture takes distresses of the heart seriously, but because it too often sends branches reaching out for anything but the Tree. Ingrown Toenails The problem comes not from a focus on the inner man. Anyone who says the Bible has little to say about internal battles, demons, depressions, anxieties, doubts, and the despairs of human life should not air his ignorance. content: The human heart is a strange and wild thing. It motivates all behavior, whether holy joys (Psalm 4:7), self-immolating sins (Matthew 15:19), or godly obedience (Ephesians 6:6). Its purposes are like deep water (Proverbs 20:5), yet it can be as shallow as a rain puddle (Matthew 13:20–21). It lives where its treasure lies (Matthew 6:21) yet wanders like a lost dog (Isaiah 63:17). Jeremiah says, “The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick” (Jeremiah 17:9). And yet for believers, a grace-born light shines there, from the face of Christ himself (2 Corinthians 4:6). A heart can be a synagogue of Satan or a tavern for the Trinity, and only sovereign grace decides. Where do this complexity and mystery leave us? How can Christians discern what’s happening inside themselves and in the hearts of those they’re discipling? The Dutch theologian Herman Bavinck said, “All of our rational and volitional life has its point of origin in the heart and is governed by it” ( The Wonderful Works of God , 3). As the most intimate part of who we are, the source for everything we think or desire, and the home of our greatest treasure, the heart is the origin of motives , the catalyst for character , and the reflection of our deepest delight . If we want to become more aware of what’s going on in our hearts and how we might shepherd the hearts of others, there are three pivotal questions we can ask: What are my motives? How am I growing in holiness? What brings me the greatest joy? The Motive Question First is the motive question, highlighted throughout the work of biblical counselor David Powlison (1949–2019). “What about motives , why people do what they do?” he asked his students. “How do we take apart their belief system, their cravings, their fears?” ( Dissecting the Heart , 80–81). Powlison spent his career building the biblical counseling movement so that Christians could address the motive question from inside the church. And in ways no secular counselor or psychologist could, he reminded us that the fundamental motive question is always God-related: The human heart has to do with God. So when the Bible describes the desires that obviously play within our souls and rule our lives, it does not portray them as hard-wired psychological or physiological givens: as needs, instincts, drives, longings, wishes. It speaks of them as morally freighted vis-à-vis God, as moral-covenantal choices: we are ruled either by cravings of the flesh or by repentance-faith-obedience to God’s desires. ( The Biblical Counseling Movement , 288) Our motives, in other words, put us into one of two orbits: a false, self-centered universe or the true, God-centered universe . As Powlison wrote, “There’s some sun around which the planet of our lives turns” ( Dissecting the Heart , 25). God is our true sun. At our best, our motives reveal that he is our deepest longing and greatest love. We want him — communion with him, growth in him, the expansion of his kingdom, and the fruition of his beautifully sovereign will. The motive question is straightforward: What is your motive? What are you chasing after, and why? Is it God, or is it something else? The greatest danger with this question is not being candid in our response. We all know what should be true. But the right answer in doctrine isn’t the same answer in devotion ; there’s a gap between head and heart. Be candid. Dig deeper. Sometimes I go three layers deep with why : What’s motivating you at work? Being noticed by others. Why? Because I want to make a name for myself. Why? Because I want my life to be significant. Why? Because I don’t fully believe that my worth and significance are found in Christ . Time to repent. Repentance is the regular and healthy behavior of a heart that gets its sense of direction from God’s word. For Christians, motive and repentance will go hand in hand for our entire lives. title: How to Commune with Christ
summary: Whether in creation, providence, redemption, or glorification, God aims to bring his people into deep fellowship with him through Jesus Christ. Watch Now
content: To understand how we commune with Christ, let’s begin at the end of history, when God’s purpose for creation and redemption and all of history has reached its climax, and then work our way back to the present so that we can see how to join God now in that ultimate purpose. That’s what gives meaning to life. That’s how you know your life counts: to know where God is taking everything and then to join him in that great achievement. So, where is history going? What is God’s ultimate purpose for all things, including you? Of course, there are millions of people who think that’s a pointless question, because the universe is not being guided. It has no purpose or goal. It is a mindless set of natural forces, moving in aimless ways that are completely random. Or “a tale told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, signifying nothing” (Macbeth 5.5.28). But God, the Creator and governor of all things, has spoken into history and told us that is not true. God has a purpose in everything, and history is going somewhere. Let me give you a litany of texts that describe where it’s going, because it’s incredibly personal and relational and communal. It’s about fellowship. God is a purposeful God. For I am God, and there is no other; I am God, and there is none like me, declaring the end from the beginning and from ancient times things not yet done, saying, “My counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish all my purpose.” (Isaiah 46:9–10) “My purpose!” God has a purpose; it’s going to stand. The LORD of hosts has sworn: “As I have planned, so shall it be, and as I have purposed, so shall it stand.” (Isaiah 14:24) In him we have obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will. (Ephesians 1:11) It is an “eternal purpose that he has realized in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Ephesians 3:11), a “purpose and grace, which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began” (2 Timothy 1:9). “The LORD has made everything for its purpose, even the wicked for the day of trouble” (Proverbs 16:4). “For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen” (Romans 11:36). So, we are not asking the wrong question when we ask, “Where is history going? What is God’s ultimate purpose for all things, including you?” That is the crucial question everyone should ask, whether we’re talking about how to commune with Jesus or anything else. Because when we know God’s ultimate purpose for the things he does, and the gifts he gives, and the obedience he requires, and we bring our life into harmony with that purpose, it’s like plugging our life into the high-voltage electric socket of God’s purpose and power and grace. And you are jolted into this realization: “My life has ultimate significance.” Ultimate. And there flows into your life confidence and joy and strength and passion, because you are linked with the ultimate purpose of God, which cannot fail. “I am God. My counsel will stand. I will accomplish all my purpose.” It is a thrilling way to live — to know where God is going, his ultimate purpose, and to join him in it. Redeemed for Fellowship with God So, when we pose the question, “How do I commune with Jesus?” we begin at the end of history, when God’s purpose for creation and redemption and all of history has reached its climax, and then work our way back and discover that communion with Jesus now is a participation in a divine purpose that is indescribably great and glorious and ultimate and eternal. What I want you to see is that the Bible describes our ultimate future as a personal relationship with Jesus, and through him with God the Father. And my emphasis is on personal. You can use different words to describe it. Our final ultimate future will be a personal relationship, or a personal fellowship, or a personal communion with Christ. “The Bible describes our ultimate future as a personal relationship with Jesus, and through him with God the Father.

content: Psalm 111:2 is one of my favorite verses in the Bible: Great are the works of the L ORD , studied by all who delight in them. Derek Kidner calls these lines “God’s charter for the scientist and artist” ( Psalms 73–150 , 432). But the scope of this charter extends far beyond the laboratory and the studio. It is the liberating banner that flies over all of Christian education. A manifesto for holy curiosity. A sovereign call to attention. Throughout Psalm 111, the anonymous author bends all his poetic effort to awaken us to the works of God so we might be alive to the God who works. He wants to pry our eyelids open with the crowbar of poetry so we might behold what God does and tremble in awe of him. He’s cleaning our lenses so that God’s works explode with clarity and color, kindling our curiosity and inspiring us to attend and adore. Doesn’t that sound wonderful? Don’t you ache to be quite awake, rather than asleep? Don’t you long to live with your eyes wide open to God and his works? If so, consider three questions Psalm 111 raises about why studying God’s works delights us. Back to School First, what does it mean to study God’s works? The word “study” ( dāraš ) means “to seek out, to experience, to attend to.” Its scope defies the confines of ivory towers or professional scholarship. The poet’s main thrust in this psalm is for you , dear reader, to study diligently in the schoolhouse of God’s works. Psalm 111:2 exhorts us to practice omnivorous attentiveness . Omnivorous describes someone who devours without discrimination, like a hungry teenager ransacking a full fridge. Those who practice omnivorous attentiveness , then, are awake to everything God does; they gobble up all his works, both the big and the small, the miraculous and the mundane. The constant exclamation of omnivorous attentiveness is “Wow, Lord, look at that !” It is the exact opposite of taking anything for granted. Those who cultivate this kind of attention live with their eyes wide open. They are awake. Wondrous Works of God But awake to what, exactly? What does Psalm 111 teach us about the scope of God’s works? The word for “works” in verse 2 means acts or creations. The term wraps its arms around all God does and says, all the fruit of his omnipotent labor. If we look at Psalm 111 as a whole, the poet leaves God’s works deliciously ambiguous. His deliverance of Israel in the exodus colors the background of this psalm, but the references are vague — intentionally so. By avoiding specifics and gesturing broadly at the wondrous works of God, our poet throws the doors wide open to omnivorous attention. He invites us to step into the entire theater of creation and redemption and marvel at the Director who runs the show. He excludes nothing from our eyes-wide-open study. Let’s follow our poet’s lead and take a brief tour through some of God’s works in this poem. General and Special Revelation To begin, verse 7 points to God’s general revelation : “The works of his hands are faithful and just.” In the Psalms, “the works of his hands” most often refers to God’s works of creation. Like an art connoisseur, our poet beckons us into the vast gallery of God’s glory to stop and admire the wonders within. Consider one example: trees. God loves trees; both his book and world are crowded with them. And no wonder! These magnificent creatures take a clear liquid, an invisible gas, and sunlight, and then — by green magic that remains a mystery to most of us — transform those ingredients into the largest, hardest, oldest living things on earth. Trees are star-powered wood towers. And time would fail to tell of children’s smiles and summer storms, eggs and honeybees, sunrises and starscapes, the extravagant green of grass and the large, slow oddity of cows. Indeed, great are the works of God! But the second half of verse 7 also highlights the privilege of God’s special revelation : “All his precepts are trustworthy.” The works of God include the words of God . General revelat

content: How old were you when you first learned that Jesus loves you? Perhaps you’ve always known it and can’t remember a day when you didn’t know the song “Jesus Loves Me” or couldn’t recite John 3:16 by heart. Maybe you were a teenager and learned about Jesus’ love through a friend or church summer camp. Or were in college and went to a concert where the gospel was clearly articulated. Maybe you were in the trenches of the workforce, and a coworker boldly shared with you about the God who radically changed their life. Regardless of how old you were, each of us who has chosen to follow Jesus has an origin story — a moment in our lives when the knowledge that “Jesus loves me, this I know, for the Bible tells me so” moved from head knowledge to heart belief. And from then on, our lives were transformed forever. This is the truth of the gospel and the power of understanding that Jesus loves you. People around the world are discovering the personal truth of John 3:16 for themselves in a language and format they clearly understand. Explore why understanding that “God so loved the world” transforms entire communities → A Changing Reality Throughout Christian history, the gospel has spread from one community to the next. Stories were told and retold, Scripture was translated, churches were planted, and discipleship deepened as people learned more about Jesus. Bible translation is foundational to all ministries of the church. It fuels evangelism, church planting, discipleship and more. It equips people to move from a blurry picture of who God is to a clear understanding and personal encounter with Jesus as Lord. Through Scripture, people are able to read, hear or see the love of God on display. Just two decades ago, most of the world’s language communities still needed Bible translation work to begin , let alone be completed. But praise God, in the last few years, we’ve seen tremendous progress made, with Bible translation underway in more languages than ever before . While the change in numbers is exciting, what’s more important is what they signify: Every number represents a person who has a story that matters to God. For these communities, the stories of future generations are being completely rewritten as children will now grow up never remembering a day when they didn’t have access to God’s Word in a language and format they clearly understand. That statement bears repeating: There will now be people who never remember a day when they didn’t have access to God’s Word in a language and format they clearly understand. From the first word of Genesis to the last word of Revelation, the Bible tells one incredible story: God’s love for the world and His invitation for people from every nation and language to know Him. Get a glimpse of how God continues writing this story today as more and more people are experiencing the power of His Word. Watch the video → A New Generation Growing Up With God’s Word Let’s take a look at some of the recent communities that are experiencing not only life transformation but generational transformation as they encounter Jesus personally through Scripture. Jakalteko | Guatemala The Jakalteko Bible was dedicated in July 2026 in Guatemala! During the celebration, John 1:1-18 was read aloud — a passage that focuses on Christ, the eternal Word and our Redeemer. Early on, many women in the community memorized Job 19 . Like Job, they had faced various hardships in their lives and identified with his suffering. The book reminded them that God remains in control and that, in the midst of difficult circumstances, their Redeemer will deliver them and comfort them in their pain. Today, they have the full counsel of God’s Word and can now see this Redeemer fulfilled in Jesus in the New Testament. They are overjoyed that the Bible has arrived in the language they were born into! When the Bible was distributed, one mother who is raising her family alone said with joy and tears: “Thank God we have the Bible in our language. Now

title: Living Out a Legacy of Stewardship and Faith
source: Wycliffe Bible Translators · 译经故事
summary: Ken and Sally discovered a way to give God’s Word — a gift they’d had access to their whole lives — to others.    The post  Living Out a Legacy of Stewardship and Faith  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
content: What did your journey to faith look like? Perhaps it was a story of how God showed up in the midst of uncertainty, doubt or fears. Maybe it involved Him seeking you out and rescuing you. Or maybe you grew up in a Christian household and your story is a bit different — perhaps your family regularly read the Bible together and have always known about Jesus’ love. Ken Trager was raised that way. He reflected, “I think when you’re raised in a Christian home … and you have the routines of a life that is built around church and prayer, you just take it for granted.” He added, “It was just the air I breathed.” For Ken and his wife, Sally, faith was always part of their stories. They were each raised in Christian homes, followed Christ, got baptized and had parents who faithfully modeled church attendance, prayer and generosity.  Ken and Sally’s paths eventually crossed at Greenville University in southern Illinois, where they met and fell in love. They went on to build a life centered around family, faith and service. Ken spent his career as a teacher and coach while Sally worked as an accountant, and together they raised two children. Now retired, they’ve moved to be closer to their children and grandchildren, giving them a new opportunity to pour into the next generation. Through all those years and seasons, the faith Ken and Sally had seen modeled by their families continued to shape their home. Early in their marriage, Ken and Sally met a mentor who encouraged the couple to go deeper with their faith — to study Scripture, ask questions and wrestle honestly with what they believed. It was an important season of discovering that the faith that had been passed down from their families could also become something they personally owned and lived out together. What Do You Take for Granted? Years later, the couple experienced an aha moment when they were introduced to Wycliffe at an event. There, Ken and Sally heard story after story from people who had received Scripture in their own languages. Something clicked for Sally: “We’ve never known a day where we couldn’t access the Bible. And these people have just longed for it, and they’re finally getting it.” For the first time, something that had always surrounded the couple became visible — and it was a gift they could no longer take for granted . Ken and Sally had spent years thinking about the importance of God’s Word. Seeing people receive Scripture in their own languages helped them understand just how extraordinary that access is. “The power of salvation comes through that,” Ken said. “I can’t think of … [a more] important work than providing God’s Word to everybody in the world.” Sally agreed. “To have His Word is as if we’re hearing the voice of God,” she said. “God works through His Word.” This conviction — for people around the world to be able to access Scripture for themselves — became one of the reasons Ken and Sally prioritized a place in their giving for Wycliffe. But it also became part of a larger question about generosity they had been asking themselves for years: “If everything we have is a gift from God, what does it look like to live generously with it?” A Generous Heart Generosity, like faith, was something Ken and Sally had grown up around. Ken remembers his dad giving him money to put in the offering plate, and Sally remembers watching her parents give not just to their church but to people and organizations in need. Sally’s father especially enjoyed giving anonymously. As Ken and Sally have grown older, they’ve learned that generosity isn’t simply about giving a certain percentage or checking a box; it’s about continually asking what it means to have a generous heart . source: Wycliffe Bible Translators · 译经故事
summary: Prayer is essential to Bible translation. Explore five specific ways to pray for local churches, translation teams and communities around the world.   The post  5 Ways to Pray for Bible Translation Around the World  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
content: Before His ascension to heaven, Jesus called the whole Church to “go and make disciples of all the nations” ( Matthew 28:18, NLT ), a command often referred to now as the Great Commission. God’s plan was to build His Kingdom in and through the Church, including local churches in every corner of the globe. And that’s exactly what’s happening today! God is on the move, and His Spirit is being poured out upon the earth in ways we’ve never seen before, particularly in the history of Bible translation. For so long, the Church was viewed as having the deepest roots and strongest influence in the West, with the West sending out Bible translators to the farthest reaches of the world. But over the last half century, the Church has exploded, expanding South and East and shifting the landscape of Bible translation with it. Johnstone Ndunde, executive director of SIL Global, a key partner of Wycliffe’s, shared: “In the world where we serve, we have many churches that have discipled, educated people [who] are able to serve the Lord as well. God’s mission is no longer from the West to the rest. It is from everyone to everywhere.” “God’s mission is no longer from the West to the rest. It is from everyone to everywhere.” This is God’s hand at work. He desires for people from every language and community to experience His redemptive power through the blood of Jesus, leading to life transformation. Scripture in a language and format they clearly understand plays a vital role in that, enabling them to know God more deeply and grow through discipleship. Today, as the Great Commission is being advanced by the global Church, local churches are taking ownership and linking arms with Wycliffe and other Bible translation agencies around the world to ensure that their communities, countries and even entire regions have God’s Word. Prayer is foundational to seeing God’s Word translated and made accessible to every person still waiting. Whether you’re praying for local churches, translation teams or communities, your prayers matter. Here are five ways you can pray for Bible translation today: Pray for Local Churches and Bible Translation Partnerships Pray for Wisdom and Strength for Bible Translation Teams Pray for Deaf Communities to Encounter Jesus Through Sign Language Pray for More People to Join the Work of Bible Translation Pray for the Translation of the Full Bible 1. Pray for Local Churches and Bible Translation Partnerships As a result of missions and technology, the gospel has spread to more communities than ever before, and now local churches worldwide are rising up to establish evangelism, discipleship, church planting and other activities in their own communities — with Bible translation central to all of those efforts! As local churches work with Bible translation organizations to translate Scripture for their own communities, that partnership is accelerating the pace of the work. This shift to local church ownership is a direct answer to decades of faithful prayer and service. Praise God! PRAY WITH US Heavenly Father, Thank You for how You are raising up men and women who not only love You but who want to be part of sharing the gospel in their own communities, countries and regions. Your love is capturing more people as they encounter You personally in a language and format they clearly understand. Equip local churches to spread Your light and love to their families and neighbors, drawing people to You through Scripture. Amen. title: Finding Wonder in the Midst of Christmas Weariness
source: Wycliffe Bible Translators · 译经故事
summary: Rediscover the wonder of Christmas by focusing on God’s faithfulness and the hope found in Jesus.   The post  Finding Wonder in the Midst of Christmas Weariness  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
content: Christmas is supposed to be a season of wonder. Twinkling lights, familiar songs, meaningful traditions and time with people you love can all point toward the joy of celebrating Jesus’ birth. But when your December calendar fills with responsibilities and expectations, weariness can settle in before you realize it. Maybe you remember a time when Christmas felt different. As a child, you may have counted down the days and experienced joy in even the smallest traditions. As an adult, you might find yourself simply trying to catch your breath as you move from one responsibility to the next. In the middle of trying to make Christmas special for everyone else, it can be easy to miss the wonder yourself. But the Christmas story gives you an opportunity to slow down and remember what this season is really about. In Luke 1, before the story of Jesus’ birth begins, you meet people who knew what it meant to wait, wonder and trust that God was at work even when they couldn’t yet see what He was doing. Weary of Waiting Luke’s account of the life of Jesus doesn’t begin with Jesus’ birth; it begins instead with the story of Zechariah, an elderly priest who was tired of waiting. Zechariah had heard promises of Israel’s rescue from oppression and sin his entire life. That future must have seemed out of reach under Rome’s harsh control. But Zechariah and his wife, Elizabeth, also had an unfulfilled personal longing: “They had no children because Elizabeth was unable to conceive, and they were both very old” ( Luke 1:7, NLT ). One day, as Zechariah performed his duties in the temple, he was chosen to burn incense in the sanctuary — a rare honor with an unexpected result: While Zechariah was in the sanctuary, an angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing to the right of the incense altar. Zechariah was shaken and overwhelmed with fear when he saw him. But the angel said, “Don’t be afraid, Zechariah! God has heard your prayer. Your wife, Elizabeth, will give you a son, and you are to name him John. You will have great joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth, for he will be great in the eyes of the Lord. He must never touch wine or other alcoholic drinks. He will be filled with the Holy Spirit, even before his birth. And he will turn many Israelites to the Lord their God. He will be a man with the spirit and power of Elijah. He will prepare the people for the coming of the Lord. He will turn the hearts of the fathers to their children, and he will cause those who are rebellious to accept the wisdom of the godly” ( Luke 1:11-17, NLT ). Trusting God in the Waiting An angel of the Lord appeared to Zechariah and announced that God had heard his prayer. Elizabeth would have a son named John who would “… prepare the people for the coming of the Lord” ( Luke 1:17b, NLT ). After years of waiting, God answered Zechariah and Elizabeth’s prayer as part of an even bigger story: They would finally have the child they had prayed for, and their son would prepare the way for Jesus. But Zechariah struggled to understand how it could possibly happen: “… ‘How can I be sure this will happen? I’m an old man now, and my wife is also well along in years’” ( Luke 1:18, NLT ). Zechariah could only see what seemed possible based on his circumstances. But God was asking him to trust what He had promised. The angel Gabriel responded by telling Zechariah that he would be unable to speak until the child was born, adding, “For my words will certainly be fulfilled at the proper time” ( Luke 1:20b, NLT ). Maybe you know what it’s like to pray about something for months or even years. It can be hard to keep trusting that God is working when it seems like nothing is changing. Zechariah’s story reminds us that even when we can’t see what God is doing, He is still faithful to His promises. Waiting is woven throughout the Christmas story. Maybe it’s part of your story too. title: No Incomplete Stories: God’s Word for All People
source: Wycliffe Bible Translators · 译经故事
summary: See how Bible translation helps communities access more of God’s Word through print, audio and sign language Scripture today.   The post  No Incomplete Stories: God’s Word for All People  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
content: Imagine reading a book, watching a show or listening to a podcast when suddenly the story just stops mid-sentence. Maybe the previous reader has ripped out a page, the series was canceled before the showrunners could wrap up the plotline, or the producer distributed the episode before realizing it was incomplete. How incredibly frustrating to not experience the full story from start to finish! It can leave us emotionally unsettled, frustrated or even distraught, because at our core, we desire completion. We want to know how things start and how they end. We don’t just want a taste, because it feels like a tease. We’re left wanting more . And we’re not alone in that desire! The same is true for communities around the world who are still waiting for the full counsel of God’s Word in a language and format they clearly understand. For some, they’re still waiting for the first verse of Scripture to be translated into their language. Others might have a few verses, chapters or Scripture portions . Still others are blessed with a complete New Testament but are waiting for the Old Testament so they can understand everything from Genesis to Revelation. They get a teaser of God’s great story — perhaps enough to understand who Jesus is and that He died for them — but they don’t have the full context as to why His sacrifice was so significant. The Bible changes everything, and together with our partners, Wycliffe believes that everyone should have access to the whole of Scripture. But don’t just take our word for it! Explore these Bible translation stories from our friends around the world who have personally experienced individual and community transformation as a result of encountering God through His Word. Want a glimpse of what it’s like to only have a portion of God’s Word? This “H ly B bl: Incomplete Scriptures” digital booklet helps you see what it’s like to have gaps in your understanding of the Bible. Explore the booklet → The Full “Outfit” of God’s Word Caroline always had access to a Bible growing up. But watching the Chonyi people of Kenya receive the New Testament in their language refreshed her passion for Bible translation, a mission she’s actively engaged in through SIL Kenya, a partner of Wycliffe. “They took a couple of Bibles, wrapped them up like a child,” she shared. “And there was a woman who was carrying the [Bibles]. And they were swinging and dancing, lifting up the [Bibles] and saying, ‘This is our child.’ Calling people, ‘Come,” in the Chonyi language. ‘Come and celebrate the child that has been born in us.’ “That is how the Chonyi people have taken the Bible — the New Testament — in their own language. That it is their child and they’re taking it seriously, making it bear fruit.” People gathered to hear Scripture read in their language, Bible studies began and the impact spread: 300 adults and 50 children gave their lives to Christ! At the celebration, the local pastors shared that now that the New Testament is complete, it’s like they have a shirt. But a shirt isn’t enough; they want a pair of pants (the Old Testament) to complete the outfit! Now work is underway to translate the Old Testament into Chonyi so that they can have the full “outfit” of God’s Word. Praise God! Watch how the Chonyi community celebrated the dedication of the New Testament in their community! As her neighbors listened alongside her, they became captivated by the story of Jesus. One day, someone from the community called the local translation office with a request. “We have been enjoying this Jesus story from this elderly woman, and now it has broken. So could you please send this device so that we could finish the whole story?” The translation team happily sent a new one, and found out that some of the people in th

title: When Generosity Becomes Worship
source: Wycliffe Bible Translators · 译经故事
summary: Discover how Millie anchored herself in God’s Word during difficult circumstances — and how that shapes her view of generosity.   The post  When Generosity Becomes Worship  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
content: What circumstances or experiences have shaped your life? For 93-year-old Millie (name changed), her testimony was shaped by the Great Depression and deep loss, but also by an enduring faith and a lifetime of seeing God’s faithfulness unfold. Every chapter of her story points back to the same truth: God’s Word sustained her. Millie was only six weeks old when her father suffered severe burns to his legs from an explosion. Overnight, Millie’s mother found herself caring for a newborn and a toddler while tending to a husband who was facing a long and painful recovery. Life was uncertain, and every dollar mattered. Yet when Millie looks back on those difficult years, she doesn’t first remember hardship. She remembers the faith that was demonstrated. Every Sunday morning, Millie’s mother would reach into a small jar where she saved a few quarters and hand one to Millie and one to her sister before they left for church. The family didn’t have much, but her parents believed that honoring God was never dependent on how much they had. “We were taught to tithe,” Millie recalled. “To give to the Lord because of His goodness to us.” Long before Millie understood phrases like “stewardship” or “planned giving,” she was learning a lesson that would shape the rest of her life: Generosity isn’t born out of abundance; it grows from trusting the one who provides. See how God is using the generosity of one group of friends to impact Bible translation → The Scripture Millie Carried Through the Years As Millie grew older, that foundation of faith continued to guide her. She married a godly man, and they centered their efforts around family, teaching and serving others. Both were educators, and they poured themselves into the lives of children while also remaining deeply involved in their church and community. Together, the couple experienced the joys of raising a family. But they also walked through a devastating loss. While Millie was pregnant with their younger son, the couple’s 7-year-old daughter tragically died. It’s difficult to imagine the depth of grief that Millie endured. Through her pain, she turned to God and His Word for comfort. Even now, decades later, she is still anchored by the promises found in Scripture. One particular passage resonates with Millie deeply: You will keep in perfect peace all who trust in you, all whose thoughts are fixed on you! Trust in the LORD always, for the LORD GOD is the eternal Rock. — Isaiah 26:3-4 (NLT) For Millie, Scripture was what met her in her grief, strengthened her through suffering and continued to anchor and guide her throughout the next chapters of her life. This past Easter, Mille’s family experienced another tragic event — her son was involved in a head-on collision. Thankfully he survived but was hospitalized and treated for serious injuries. Millie believes the Lord’s presence was unmistakable in the moments that followed this event. A Gift Rooted in Gratitude Not long after her son’s accident, Millie received a mailing from Wycliffe Foundation that included information about charitable gift annuities. For Millie, this felt like an invitation and an opportunity to respond to God’s faithfulness through generosity. A charitable gift annuity was not a completely new concept to Millie. Through family members connected with Faith Comes By Hearing (a Wycliffe partner organization), she learned about this unique giving option and appreciated that it could provide her with a lifetime income while also supporting a ministry she cared deeply about. When she received the information about charitable gift annuities, she saw it as another opportunity to worship the Lord and express her gratitude for His protection and provision. Millie reached out to Wycliffe Foundation, and Michael Occhipinti, senior gift planning advisor, quickly connected with her. He walked alongside her throughout the process as she prayerfully considered her next step. For Millie, establishing a charitable gift annuity became ano

content: April Bunn, IMB director of global prayer strategies, shows messengers at an SBC annual meeting the latest Loving the Lost prayer resource. IMB Photo April Bunn directs global prayer strategies for the IMB. IMB Photo My husband and I moved from our home in Tennessee to South Asia when we were in our 20s. God called us to serve overseas through the International Mission Board, and we were excited to share the gospel with those who had not yet had an opportunity to hear it. As we began to plant our lives in a city on the other side of the world, we quickly realized the task before us was massive. We were surrounded by millions of people, the vast majority of whom were spiritually lost and on a trajectory to an eternity separated from Christ. We were grappling with a new language, a different culture, unfamiliar foods, homesickness and the list went on. We were overwhelmed. The reality of the lostness around us felt too much to carry. As we turned to God for help, He reminded us that we were not meant to carry this task alone. We had been sent as laborers to the nations, but the Great Commission was given to the whole Church. The Church was our partner in this work. As we began intentionally inviting brothers and sisters in the U.S. to walk with us regularly in prayer, we saw God move in unmistakable ways. They carried the burden of lostness with us, and they also rejoiced with us as we saw God work. We had been sent as laborers to the nations, but the Great Commission was given to the whole Church. The Church was our partner in this work. Today, after two decades in South Asia, I have the privilege of encouraging and equipping believers to pray for people and places around the world through my work with the IMB. In doing so, I’m continually reminded that God’s mission is His work, and we are utterly dependent on Him to accomplish it. Missionaries can faithfully go, learn languages, share the gospel and disciple believers, but they cannot change hearts. God can. That is why we ask you to pray. Prayer is strategic to the Great Commission, and e very believer can take part in it. As the Church, we are living between the giving of the Great Commission and its culmination in the great multitude we see in Revelation 7:9, where people from every nation, tribe, people and language will stand before the throne worshiping God together. Until that day, we go to take the good news to a world in need. And we pray, asking God to do what only He can do. Through prayer, every believer, regardless of age or location, can intercede for places we may never be able to go ourselves. No country or people group is closed to the work of the Spirit through the prayers of God’s people. We may not see every answer to those prayers in our lifetime; some will only become visible when we stand before the throne and see the faces of those God drew to Himself. Until then, we keep praying. April Bunn, IMB director of global prayer strategies, shows messengers at an SBC annual meeting the latest Loving the Lost prayer resource. The new Loving the Lost is available for free from the IMB. IMB Photo Paul tells us in Colossians 4:2 to “continue steadfastly in prayer, being watchful in it with thanksgiving.” To be watchful means we are paying attention and expecting God to work. The Mixtec people of Mexico have reminded me what that kind of watchful, steadfast prayer looks like. Beginning in 2008, IMB missionaries serving among the Mixtec began sharing prayer requests with IMB’s prayer office so they could be shared widely and more believers could join them in prayer. The requests were simple. Pray for open hearts. Pray for opportunities to share Bible stories in the Mixtec language. Pray for people to help make Scripture accessible. Pray for God to open doors. Month after month and year after year, people prayed for access to villages, for the first believers, for courage in the face of persecution. Today there is a growing fellowship of Mixtec believers. content: An IMB missionary among the Deaf records a Bible story in sign language. IMB Photo Every dollar you give to the Lottie Moon offering goes to support missionaries like Noah Lewis who live and serve among the lost. Will you consider giving today? Noah Lewis couldn’t help signing along with a worship song playing in the background as Deaf friends gathered in his home for dinner. The International Mission Board appoints missionaries who are both Deaf and hearing to serve among the global Deaf. Many missionaries learn sign language for the first time, while others use their American Sign Language to more quickly learn global sign languages. IMB Photo The International Mission Board missionary was sitting in the living room with his roommate and two friends while others prepared food nearby. As a young, single adult, simply opening the doors to his home in the Middle East has created some of his most fruitful opportunities for gospel conversations. That evening, Lewis was stirred to worship the Lord. “I just love worshiping in sign language because it’s a full-body experience,” Lewis said. Lewis, who is hearing, began signing the song in American Sign Language. Across the room, one of his Muslim friends watched intently. When the song ended, his friend told him it was beautiful and asked to see another. Lewis explained that Christians use songs to worship God. His friend compared what he had seen to hearing the Islamic call to prayer. The exchange opened an opportunity for Lewis to explain Christian worship and why Christians worship Jesus. When his friend asked to see more, Lewis continued signing songs from the playlist. “He was just really captivated by it,” Lewis said. “It really felt like in that moment the Spirit was working in his heart.” The conversation did not end with a profession of faith. Instead, it became another step in a friendship where Lewis has watched spiritual curiosity grow over time. During Ramadan, the same friend asked about fasting. On another night, he asked how Christians pray. Each question has allowed Lewis to explain what Christians believe and why he follows Jesus. Those conversations reflect much of Lewis’ ministry. He has served in the Middle East for nearly a year and a half, spending much of his time learning sign language and building relationships in the local Deaf community. Learning sign language, like learning any language, requires time, practice and immersion in the community that uses it. For Lewis, that process has looked different from the experience of missionaries who can spend several hours each day in a formal language school. There are no comparable sign language centers where he serves, so much of his language learning happens through relationships with Deaf friends. Although Lewis has not had a dedicated language tutor since arriving on the field, personal relationships help him develop a strong conversational understanding of the sign language used where he serves. The process has also drawn him more deeply into the Deaf community he came to reach. “I want to genuinely learn about their language,” he said. “I want to be friends with them. I want to know who they are.” As Lewis’ ability to communicate grows, relationships deepen and opportunities to share the gospel follow. Even when he doesn’t know the exact sign he needs, friends help him find ways to communicate biblical truths. Lewis has learned to faithfully use the language he has while continuing to grow in his ability to communicate the gospel clearly. An IMB worker among the Deaf records a Bible story. Generous giving to the Lottie Moon Christmas Offering supports missions among the global Deaf. Lewis currently lives and serves in the Middle East, but he arrived on the field with a long-term desire to serve in Central Asia. title: Ohio Sending Celebration affirms 33 IMB missionaries for global service
summary: God continues to call His people to carry the gospel to the ends of the earth. During a Sending Celebration Nov. 9 at the Sugarcreek Campus of First Baptist Church Kettering, near Dayton, Ohio, 33 International Mission Board missionaries stood before family, friends and supporters, affirming their obedience to that call. Trustees of the IMB appointed the fully supported missionaries who represent 10 states – including two candidates from Ohio – and many Southern Baptist churches committed to sen
content: Participants at the IMB Sending Celebration on Nov. 9, 2026, celebrated God's faithfulness in sending 33 new missionaries to the nations. Held at the Sugarcreek campus of First Baptist Kettering near Dayton, Ohio, the event launched the State Convention of Baptists in Ohio annual gathering. For security reasons, some newly appointed missionaries are not publicly identified. IMB Photo God continues to call His people to carry the gospel to the ends of the earth. During a Sending Celebration Nov. 9 at the Sugarcreek Campus of First Baptist Church Kettering, near Dayton, Ohio, 33 International Mission Board missionaries stood before family, friends and supporters, affirming their obedience to that call. Trustees of the IMB appointed the fully supported missionaries who represent 10 states – including two candidates from Ohio – and many Southern Baptist churches committed to sending and sustaining those called by God to go to the mission field. Senior Pastor Chad Keck welcomed those in attendance, sharing his appreciation for the partnership with Southern Baptist churches to cooperatively send and support missionaries. The Sending Celebration is meeting in conjunction with the State Convention of Baptists in Ohio. Chad Keck, senior pastor of First Baptist Kettering near Dayton, Ohio, left, and Jeremy Westbrook, executive director-treasurer of the State Convention of Baptists in Ohio, right, welcome guests gathered for the IMB Sending Celebration, which kicked off the convention’s annual gathering. IMB Photo Among those who shared their stories include a couple who answered an unexpected call later in life, a couple who are returning to Albania and to people they could not forget; and a couple who moved from welcoming the nations in Canada to going to Fiji. All of them shared their stories before the Sending Celebration. Unexpected invitation to go On Dec. 5, 2025, what seemed like an ordinary FaceTime call became a turning point for Rob Boss. As he spoke with his daughter, Hannah, during her IMB training, Rob sensed God speaking clearly to his heart: “You can do this too.” The impression was unexpected. After decades of writing, Christian education, seminary teaching and active support of missions, overseas service had never been part of Rob and Stephanie Boss’ plans. “It wasn’t an audible voice, but it was so clear,” Rob said. “It was Him. It was so kind and so gentle and so encouraging.” The moment drove him to his knees in surrender. When Stephanie came home later that day, he told her he believed God was calling them to the nations. Her response was immediate. “Thrilled is the right answer,” she said. The next day, the couple contacted the IMB and began the application process. Though missions had long been part of their family’s story, Rob and Stephanie Boss sensed God leading them to overseas service while encouraging their daughter, Hannah, during her missionary training. Sent by Wedgwood Baptist Church in Fort Worth, Texas, they are now headed to Colombia, where they will serve through theological education. IMB Photo Looking back, the Bosses see the Lord’s hand preparing them long before they realized where He was leading. “God brought us together in the summer of 1990 at Glorieta, New Mexico, where we met and married,” Stephanie said during the Sending Celebration. What followed was years of ministry, teaching, parenting and navigating life’s unexpected turns, which taught them to hold plans loosely and trust God completely. “We did not have a clue about what life held in front of us,” Stephanie said. “We just knew we wanted to follow the Lord.” Their calling also continues a family legacy. Rob’s mother served with the IMB in Africa after retirement, helping inspire Hannah’s service in South Korea. Now, three generations of the same family have answered God’s call to the nations. Rob and Stephanie expressed deep gratitude for their sending church, Wedgwood Baptist Church in Fort Worth, whose strong commitment to missions

title: IMB missionaries in place, prepared to encourage Senegal’s churches toward Youth Olympics outreach
summary: As athletes and spectators from around the world fill the streets of Senegal for the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games, missionaries and local believers are praying the event will leave behind more than medals and memories. For Carson West, an International Mission Board missionary serving in Senegal, the Games represent a unique opportunity not only to engage visitors with the gospel but also to mobilize local churches to take a more active role in evangelism long after the Olympic flame is exting
content: A Senegalese Christian shares the gospel with event volunteers during the Youth Olympic Games in Dakar. IMB Photo As athletes and spectators from around the world fill the streets of Senegal for the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games, missionaries and local believers are praying the event will leave behind more than medals and memories. For Carson West, an International Mission Board missionary serving in Senegal, the Games represent a unique opportunity not only to engage visitors with the gospel but also to mobilize local churches to take a more active role in evangelism long after the Olympic flame is extinguished. “This is the first Olympic event ever held on the continent of Africa,” West said. “For us, it was an opportunity to ask, ‘What are we going to do with this?’” The Youth Olympic Games, which began Oct. 31 and end Nov. 13, are taking place across three host cities: Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly. Event organizers expect nearly 2,700 athletes, ages 14-17, to participate in 35 sports and represent more than 200 delegations. The Games have drawn a million spectators, and West reported more than 6,000 event volunteers are staffing all the venues. With so many people gathering in Senegal, West and his team concentrated on preparing Senegalese churches for evangelistic opportunities. “We could run and hide, or we could do this thing,” West said, recalling an early conversation with teammates. “We decided we were going to do this thing.” The 2026 Youth Olympic Games in Dakar, Senegal, is the first Olympic event held on the continent of Africa. IMB Photo West serves as team leader for IMB work in Senegal, where ministry efforts focus on three areas: gospel engagement, church advancement and community development. The Youth Olympic outreach naturally aligns with the first two priorities. “Our approach has been to mobilize the local church,” he said. “This is their backyard.” Instead of relying on a large influx of international volunteers, though there is one volunteer team from the United States serving, the strategy has centered on equipping local believers. Senegal has four Baptist churches in the greater Dakar area. Many leaders representing the congregations, as well as other ministry partners, participated in evangelism training designed specifically for the Games. Church leaders and ministry partners in Senegal participate in an evangelism training session specifically designed to share the gospel during the Youth Olympic Games in Dakar. IMB Photo A key outreach method involves trading commemorative pins, a familiar Olympic tradition. Volunteers use the exchange as a natural conversation starter before offering gospel-centered materials. Each pin is accompanied by a card featuring a QR code connected to a digital engagement platform adapted from previous Olympic and World Cup outreaches. Visitors who scan the code are directed to online resources and can connect with trained digital responders. Experienced volunteers in the U.S. are helping provide follow-up conversations. “We’re building on strategies that have been used effectively in previous Olympic Games,” West said. “It’s an easy, non-intimidating way to start gospel conversations.” Trading commemorative pins is an Olympic tradition. Volunteers use these pins to start gospel-driven conversations during the Youth Olympic Games in Dakar. Each pin is accompanied by a card featuring a QR code that connects people to trained digital responders. IMB Photo The effort extends beyond Dakar. IMB teams and church partners are positioned in each of the three host cities. An IMB team, which includes three global missionary partners, is helping coordinate outreach efforts in Diamniadio, and an IMB team along with a Baptist church is organizing efforts in Saly. West believes the greatest potential impact may be felt not among international visitors but among Senegalese believers themselves. Senegal is approximately 95% Muslim and 0.2% evangelical.
